ivc_1: A device alarms once 4 of its last 6 windows reach the threshold. We pick the lowest threshold at which benign devices stay under 0.01 false alarms per hour across 80 hours of long simulated sessions (Section VI-B). A second gate, also using a 4-of-6 count, triggers when a keyboard sends 30 or more reports per second, a rate no human reached in our population of 1,972, where the maximum sustained was 26 (Section V-A). Either gate can raise an alarm (logical OR), matching our evaluation setup.
ivc_2: Two checks determine what gets judged at all. First, the model records the interface classes of its benign training devices. A device that declares any other class, such as a network adapter, a serial converter, or a smart-card reader, is reported as unmodelled: it is scored and stored, but never escalated. Second, for HID interfaces the class alone isn't enough, because a keyboard and a tablet share it. What a HID interface can actually send is declared in its report descriptor [18], which the kernel exposes in sysfs. Keystrokes require the Keyboard page, and applications can be launched through the Consumer page. Any device that may send keystrokes is always judged, even when its descriptor can't be read. A pure pointer falls outside the threat model and is reported as unmodelled.
ivd_1: When a device is escalated, the system generates THROTTLE and then DEAUTHORIZE actions, each with the kernel command and the evidence behind it, and stores them. Nothing is actually written to the kernel's authorization interface. Execution is gated behind a manual safety review that hasn't been done yet, so the claim of closed-loop enforcement remains untested. The monitor and an operator API run as hardened systemd services, and each checkpoint carries a fixed-input fingerprint that the loader verifies.
va_intro: No labelled USB attack traffic is public, so our training data come from a simulator that writes sessions in usbmon's exact text format, and the same parser reads them back. Benign devices are drawn from five profiles: keyboard, mouse, mass storage, webcam, and audio. The choices that matter, and their sources, are:
va_b1: Typing speed: each device draws its own median interkey time, log-uniform over 60 to 300 ms, with log-normal spread.
va_b2: Key releases: as the HID boot protocol specifies, every keystroke sends a key-down and a key-up report, and overlapping keys produce multi-key reports. Key holds are log-normal with a median of 90 ms.
va_b3: Text: a Zipf-weighted vocabulary whose digram entropy is tuned to 3.56 bits, Shannon's estimate for English [19].
va_b4: Idle periods: 40% of benign devices are always active, 15% pause for 3 to 8 s between bursts, 15% for 8 to 20 s, 20% for 20 to 60 s, and 10% sit idle after enumeration.
va_b5: Session length and attack onset: every session, benign or attack, lasts 40 to 85 s. Onset falls at 1.5 to 4 s for injection, 15 to 30 s for the identity switch, 45 to 62% of the session for the staged attack, 5 to 12 s for covert exfiltration, and 4 to 12 s for the mimicry families. A human-paced payload is 60 to 220 keys.
va_three: Three choices keep the attacks from being easy. Attack devices draw their timing persona from the same prior as benign ones, the mimicry families draw keystroke timing from the exact human parameters, and benign and attack sessions share a single duration distribution. A leakage audit tests duration, window count, and identifier for each family; it found a time-since-enumeration leak, which is now excluded.
va_tableref: Table IV compares the simulator against real people: the 1,972 participants of the 136M Keystrokes study [20] and the 51 subjects of the CMU benchmark [21]. The simulator types at a realistic median pace and hold time, but it pauses more than transcription typists and has no very fast typists. This is why we take the capability bound from the real data.
va_illustration: For illustration, two seconds of a benign keyboard produce lines such as C Ii:3:003:1 0:10 8 = 00000b00…, spaced a few dozen milliseconds apart. Each key-down report is followed by its all-zero release. Machine-speed injection emits the same pairs only about 2 ms apart, and keeps going for as long as its payload lasts. The model card lists real excerpts of both.
vb_1: Corpus A is the original corpus: 1,000 sessions, 600 of them benign, in which every benign device is always active. Corpus B has the same size and seed but uses the realistic generator from Section V-A, and the deployed model is trained on it. Corpus C is a fresh set of 3,600 sessions (3,000 benign and 100 per attack family) drawn from a different seed and never used to train, calibrate, or select anything. Splits are made by session, never by window: 30% of each profile is held out for testing, and 20% of the remainder is drawn for validation, which is where thresholds are set (Table V). The long-session sets used for calibration and evaluation have their own seeds.
vc_1: To test on real kernels, we boot four distributions headless under QEMU with hardware acceleration: Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8), Debian 13 (6.12), Fedora 44 (6.19), and AlmaLinux 9 (5.14). Each guest has 11 emulated USB devices: a boot keyboard, a mouse, an absolute tablet, a pen tablet, bulk-only and UAS storage, audio, a network adapter, a serial converter, a smart-card reader, and a hub. The kernels and drivers are real; only the device side is emulated. The keyboard replays the key-down and key-up times of real participants [20], and the mouse and tablet replay the Balabit recordings of ten users [22]. On a seeded schedule, the guest copies files to the drives, sends network packets, writes to the serial port, and plays audio.
vc_2: Each distribution runs one 75-minute benign session and two 30-minute attack sessions. In the attack sessions, six episodes are played on newly attached keyboards: the five attack families a keyboard can carry out, plus a benign control in which a new keyboard is used by a replayed person. Attack payloads are innocuous text without the Enter key, so what makes them attacks is the traffic the kernel sees. Captures are scored through the deployed monitor loop itself, replayed as fast as the file can be read. A test confirms that this fast replay gives the same verdicts as replay at wall-clock pace.
vd_1: Rates carry 95% Wilson intervals or counts. LSTM training is seed-sensitive, so comparisons that could hinge on the seed use three seeds, and a difference counts only if it exceeds both the seed spread and one session. Every candidate improvement had its adoption criterion written into its script before the first run, and two failed (Section VI-E). Every number here is read from a file written by a seeded script in the project repository, and this document is generated from those files. Seeds: 7 for Corpora A and B and model training (8 and 9 for spread), 2025 for Corpus C, 4049 for threshold calibration, 2027 to 2031 for the long-session evaluation sets, and 1 and 2 for the testbed rounds. The code, data formats and generator settings are in the repository and its model card; the human-input datasets are fetched from their publishers under their licences and are not redistributed.
via_1: On Corpus A, the full system detected 107 of 120 attack sessions (89.2%) with no false positives across 178 benign test sessions, compared with 15.8% without the LSTM. That result did not survive realism. Corpus A's benign devices never go idle, and once they did, the same model flagged 46.6% of Corpus B's benign sessions. After retraining on Corpus B, the model at its original per-window threshold detects 496 of 600 attacks (82.7%) in Corpus C, with 2 false positives in 3,000 benign sessions. At the deployed, calibrated threshold, it detects 448 of 600 (74.7%) with no false positives (Table VI).
abstract: USB hosts trust what a peripheral declares, so a BadUSB device that declares itself a keyboard can type a payload seconds after it is plugged in. IUDBMS judges devices by behaviour instead. It reads the Linux usbmon stream, summarises each device second as 30 features, scores them with an Isolation Forest and an LSTM over ten second sequences, and alarms when four of six seconds look malicious. Enforcement is generated but not applied, and the models are trained on simulated traffic, so the work is a simulation based proof of concept. On 3,600 fresh simulated sessions, with the alarm threshold calibrated to 0.01 false alarms per device hour, it detects 448 of 600 attack sessions (74.7%) with no false alarm in 3,000 benign ones. A typing speed bound measured on 1,972 people raises detection of attack families withheld from training from 34.8% to 68.2%. On four Linux distributions with emulated devices driven by recorded human input, none of 114 benign devices alarmed in 41 device hours and 24 of 24 fast injection attacks were caught, but by the speed bound. The learned model alone caught 1 of 40, and human paced attacks went undetected.
index_terms: BadUSB, behavioural anomaly detection, false alarms per device hour, HID, Isolation Forest, LSTM, USB security, usbmon.
contrib_1: A working pipeline (implemented): capture, features, a two stage detector, a gated policy, storage, dashboard and systemd services, running on real kernels. Enforcement is generated but not applied.
contrib_2: Setting the alarm threshold: The usual estimate of 1 in 10,000 was off by a factor of millions because the alamrs don't become rare with individual suspicious seconds being rare. On long simulated sessions a keyboard falsely alarmed about every four to five hours. Upon direct alarm rate measurement, it was found that the threshold is the lowest one and gives one false alarm per 100 hours across 80 hours of simulated normal use on average and keyboard false alarms reduced from 0.225 an hour to 0.013 an hour. On real kernels, none of 12 keyboards replaying real people's typing alarmed, where 6 of 12 did at the old threshold.
contrib_3: A typing speed limit taken from 1,972 real people is used as a second alarm beside the model. Because it needs no training on attacks, it catches fast attacks the model was never trained on, raising detection of unseen attack types from 34.8% to 68.2%; human speed attacks remain undetected.
contrib_4: A test setup running real Linux kernels (four distributions) with 11 kinds of emulated USB device, driven by recordings of real people's typing and mouse use. It showed two things: the learned model, trained on simulated traffic, could not be set to catch attacks on real kernels without also raising false alarms; and refusing to judge device types the model was never trained on removed all false alarms on normal devices while every device able to type was still checked.
contrib_5: Negative results with their pre registered criteria, including two candidate improvements that were measured and not adopted.
intro_1: A USB host believes what a device says about itself. During enumeration the device reports its vendor and product identifiers and its interfaces, and the host binds drivers to them with no attestation. BadUSB [1] turns this into an attack. Reprogrammed firmware lets a flash drive or a cable declare a keyboard and type a stored payload as soon as it is plugged in. The operating system treats those keystrokes as a person’s, so the payload runs with the user’s privileges.
intro_2: Defences in use today check identity. Allowlists admit devices by class and identifier [2], GoodUSB asks the user which functions a device should have [3], and USBFILTER enforces packet rules in the USB stack [4]. A device that copies an allowed identity passes all of them. Behavioural monitors exist for keystrokes [5], [6], but they are rule or threshold based, and the learned temporal models that work well for network intrusion detection [7]–[11] have not been applied to the event stream of a single USB device. Where learned detectors are evaluated, the figures are per window or per short session on synthetic or benchmark traffic. A monitor watches each device for a working day, so the number that matters to an operator is false alarms per device hour, and a model trained on simulated USB traffic has to be checked against real kernel output before any result means much.
intro_3: IUDBMS is our attempt to close that gap, and this paper reports how far it gets. It is a Linux monitor that reads every USB request block (URB) through usbmon, scores each device once a second, and escalates through a persistence gate. The contributions are listed once here, each with the scope of its evidence:
related_a1: Shen et al. [2] proposed WMUD, a server side allowlist for USB redirection to virtual desktops. It keys policy on class and identifier, which shows the value of tamper resistant policy but admits any device that presents an allowed identity. GoodUSB [3] mediates the Linux USB stack and grants a device only the functions the user expects. USBFILTER [4] filters packets between drivers and the host controller at a cost of microseconds per packet. These are identity or rule based.
related_a2: Closer to our setting, SafeUSB [5] monitors keystrokes on Windows with an inter keystroke timing threshold and keyword matching, and reports roughly one second between con nection and the start of monitoring. USBlock [6] detects injection devices from the timing of the packets they send, and Huang et al. [12] identify HID attacks from host process events. As far as we can tell from their descriptions, none of these learns a per device model or models a device’s behaviour over a sequence of windows, and none reports false alarms per device hour.
via_2: Every single time at either threshold 4 families are detected but the cost of calibration only falls on one family, the replay loop, which drops from 95% to 48%; the single human-paced payload is not detected by anything. The capability gate alone reaches 400/600 (66.7%) with no false positive and adds nothing to the deployed rule on families the model was trained on. In our earlier study three hand-written rules reached the same 66.7% in simulation but what learning adds over rules is the replay loop.
vib_1: A per-window false-positive rate of 10⁻⁴ was set on the validation windows’ threshold. On sessions of up to an hour (about 101 device-hours) that model raised 0.149 false alarms per keyboard-hour, about one per keyboard per working day, and none on other classes; short sessions had too few hours to show it. Table VII explains why the per-window target says little. About 1.05e-03 of windows on 40 benign keyboard-hours were over that threshold, ten times the target, because the pooled validation target hides the own rate of the keyboard. Since consecutive LSTM inputs share nine of ten rows, an over-threshold window was followed around 38% of the time. The normally observed alarms per hour is 0.255 but the treating windows as independent predicts 6.5e-08 alarms per hour.
vib_2: We therefore choose the threshold on gate firings. Each The largest critical threshold of a session is where its gate fires, so the whole curve of false alarms against threshold is a sort; this is tested against the policy engine. The smallest threshold with atleast 0.01 alarms per-device was adopted after 80 hours of long benign sessions from a calibration seed, as pre-registered, and evaluated once on a fresh seed: keyboard false alarms fell from 0.225 to 0.013 per hour, at the cost in Table VI. The full threshold curve is in the result file, so a deployment can trade the other way.
vic_1: Stage 2 learns the families it is shown. Mean detection on Corpus C falls from 82.7% to 34.8% when it is trained without a family and trained on it. To see why, we trained on benign traffic and one family at a time and tested every family (Table VIII).
vic_2: The two human-paced families transfer to and from nothing while the four injection-speed families transfer among themselves almost completely. The features that separate its attack windows from benign windows of the same class by Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of at least 0.8 was measured for each family. The overlap of those sets predicts transfer (Spearman ρ = +0.61; a version using the top five features, stated before the run, gave −0.22 because many features tie at 1.00). Mostly rate and timing were shared along with 9 to 11 such features between families. The human-paced families have none: their best feature reaches 0.45.A new human-paced attack will not be caught by training on old ones because a supervised model can only learn weak, family-specific cues for them, and no other family carries those cues.
vic_3: The capability gate needs no training family. Combined with the model under the same leave-one-family-out protocol, mean detection rises from 34.8% to 68.2%: identity switch and covert exfiltration go from 0% to 100%, with no added false positive, because they inject at machine speed. The human-paced families stay where they were.
vid_1: The parser read 2,901,742 lines from four kernels with 0 unparsed (Table IX). Ubuntu lacks usbmon until an extra module package is installed and along with this Ubuntu’s and Fedora’s cloud kernels ship without the audio, network and serial lass drivers so the same emulated devices fall silent after enumeration and this is where the environment differs in a way simulation can not show.
vid_t1: Table X holds the main real-kernel result. No alarm was raised on any of the 114 benign device sessions over 41.4 device-hours, this includes 12 keyboards driven by real people’s keystrokes, and detected with a median latency of 2.6s all the 24 injected-speed attacks. Those detections are the capability gate’s.1 out of 40 attacks were caught at its calibrated threshold by the learned model alone(†, competence checks on). 24 injection attacks were caught but it also alarmed on 6 of the 12 human-typed keyboards at the per-window threshold(‡, every device judged). Unlike the simulator’s 390 the real injection polled every 10ms through a keyboard, and the model’s score reached the calibrated threshold too briefly to complete the gate.  The human-paced attacks(0/16) were not detected by anything except the original Corpus-A model, which alarmed on 82 of the 114 benign devices.
vid_2: The competence checks were needed. Judging every device, the same model alarmed on 27 benign devices: a network adapter whose link-status endpoint sends an identical eight-byte report every 32 ms (perfectly regular and repetitive, which is what injection looks like to a model that has only seen keyboards), a serial converter, hubs, and the absolute tablet, whose six-byte reports no training device had. The HID check was designed after seeing the tablet alarm and validated on the sessions run afterwards.
vie_1: Sample-size-robust features. Windows holding one keystroke, where the coefficient of variation and entropy of inter-arrival times are exactly zero, the signature of the script , were from where most of the long session false alarms came from. Freezing either feature removed every such alarm in the trained model. Retraining with versions shrunk toward a Poisson prior, and with a novelty feature on a 60-second horizon, did not: pooled over three seeds the candidate raised more keyboard alarms than the base model (0.296 against 0.242 per hour), so it was not adopted.
vie_2: Polling-limited injection. Training on injection bounded by a device polling interval of 1 to 10 ms, after the real-kernel miss, lowered Corpus C detection to 71.5% (replay loop 29%) and caught almost none of the real-kernel attacks, failing two of its four criteria. The sim-to-real gap is not only speed.
vie_3: Earlier negative results. The per-device baseline contributes nothing measurable, even when devices are made heterogeneous; 13 alternative alerting rules, a long-repeat feature, longer context and a five-seed ensemble all fall within seed noise; a host-level feature for concurrent mouse activity did not help, because simulated devices on one host are independent. The usbmon timestamp wraps at 4,096 s and the parser had assumes 2³² µs, shifting every event after a wrap 199 s into the future, and the descriptor scanner had marked every real interface as late arriving, these were the two real defects surfaced on real kernels.
vif_1: The streaming detector costs 3.8 ms per device-window, about 264 devices per core. An eBPF probe on the URB completion hook counts exactly the same completions as usbmon (1,144 of 1,144 under load), but reads the URB status too early to be correct, emits no records and is not a capture backend.
vif_2: Table XI measures each monitor on a guest whose storage stick is driven with 4 KiB direct I/Os, so that every few kilobytes costs three URBs, the worst case for a per-URB monitor. Since a first version of the benchmark drifted by more than any difference between conditions, each condition is compared with the unmonitored run of the same repetitions. No monitor’s cost is detectable. 7 of 8 intervals contain zero; the rest of them lie on the other side where monitoring would make transfers faster, which no monitor can cause, and it expected to miss with 8 intervals at 95%. The resolution is coarse, ±10 to 30%, because the device is emulated, so the honest statement is an upper bound, not a zero. 3.8 µs per URB completion is the value of the kernel’s own BPF statistics in this guest, this is the same for counting and per-event output, which suggests the measurement’s own timing dominates; at a keyboard’s ten or so URBs a second that is negligible.
vii_1: Table XII separates what was proposed, what was built and what the experiments support. The four novelty claims of the original proposal are N1 to N4.
vii_2: Three readings follow. The first is that the strongest  result is operational: a monitor that raised no false alarm on 114 real-kernel device sessions and caught every injection-speed attack, with the detections coming from a physical bound and the learned model contributing its calibrated restraint rather than its detections. Second, even in simulation the learned model’s advantage is narrow and it did not carry over to real kernel traffic, so this paper does not present IUDBMS as a detector of unknown attacks. Third, statistically the same process as a person typing within one device’s traffic is how the human-paced payload types once ; no feature we have separates it, and no detector here catches it.
verify_limitations: 1) Simulated training data. Every model is trained on simulated traffic, and the real-kernel results show that the learned component does not transfer at a usable operating point. 2) Emulated devices and recorded users. The testbed’s kernels and drivers are real, but the devices are QEMU’s and the input is replayed, not live. No physical device, real attack hardware or live user has been tested. A capture tool that pseudonymises payloads as it records exists for contributors with their own machines and devices; no contribution has been analysed yet. 3) Small real-kernel attack set. Forty episodes, eight per family, on one QEMU keyboard model with a 10 ms polling interval. A device declaring a slower interval, or typing just under 30 reports per second, would evade the capability gate. 4) Human-paced attacks are not detected. Neither the model nor the gate catches a payload typed at human speed. 5) Enforcement is not applied. Actions are generated and logged only, so the closed loop and its latency are untested. 6) Assumptions in the generator. Idle mixes, text model and onsets are our choices; the replay-loop result swings from 97% to 1% on one attacker choice. 7) Post-hoc design. The HID competence check and the 0.8 overlap threshold were introduced after seeing data; both are reported as such, and the check was validated only on sessions run after it was designed.
verify_conclusion: IUDBMS treats USB trust as a question about behaviour over time. As built, it is a working Linux monitor whose alarm threshold is set in false alarms per device-hour, which declines to judge device types its model never saw, and which pairs a learned sequence model with a bound on human typing speed. In simulation it detects 448/600 (74.7%) of fresh attack sessions at no false positive in 3,000 benign ones. On four real kernels it raised no false alarm in 41 device-hours and caught every injection-speed attack, but those detections came from the typing-speed bound, and human-paced attacks went undetected. The work is a simulation-based proof of concept with a real-kernel testbed, not a tested security product. The next steps are recordings of real users on physical devices, real attack hardware, a review of the enforcement path before it touches a kernel, and features that can see a human-paced payload.
